hindsight: Key rig facts I wish I had at the start: (1) Each move_to call only executes a few control steps (about 3-10 mm of motion) UNLESS the gripper command changes by a large amount, in which case the call runs about 80 steps (4 s) and the position servo converges to its commanded target - so pad position commands should be paired with a large gripper change (e.g. gripper 1 together with z=0.81) to actually reach a pose. (2) eef_pos sits near the fingertip/grasp-site level: commanding z=0.846 left the pads level with the block top (block top about 0.843), so a real top-down grasp needs eef z about 0.81-0.82 where the pads straddle roughly 30 mm of the block sides. (3) In the wrist view the finger-gap center is at u about 112; world +x maps to image-down (about 0.9 px/mm at 8 cm above the table) and world +y maps to image-right (about 0.85 px/mm), so lateral offsets can be measured in pixels while the object is inside the wrist frame. (4) The fixed front and side cameras both showed the gripper looking just above the block at every height and at 15-40 mm lateral offset, so they cannot be used to fine-align in x/y; only the wrist camera plus the measured eef_pos can. (5) In this scene the block sits near (x about -0.02, y about 0.015) and the blue bowl about 10 cm away at (x about +0.08, y about 0) - but the block drifts a few mm per failed close as the pads brush it, so re-verify its position in the wrist view before each attempt instead of trusting an earlier estimate. (6) Budget roughly: locate 2 calls, descend+close at least 3 calls (the z descent is slow unless padded by a gripper command), lift+traverse 2 calls, release 1 call; plan the whole placement before spending calls on probing.

hindsight: Concrete facts measured in this trial. (1) Chunk length: the move_to step count is set by the largest normalised delta including the gripper dimension, so re-issuing gripper=0 or gripper=1 from the opposite extreme buys 40-79 step chunks (2-4 s) while a small pure Cartesian move gives only 1-3 steps; the arm does reach the commanded pose when the chunk is long, and lags about 1 cm per 3-step chunk otherwise. (2) The gripper stroke is slow, roughly 0.006-0.012 normalised per step, so a full open-to-close needs on the order of 60-120 control steps: plan at least two long chunks for a close. (3) The red block is about 4 cm across: a genuine grip stalls the measured opening near 0.50-0.52 and then holds through lift and transport; if the reading keeps falling past 0.4 down to 0.02-0.3 the pads closed on air. (4) Fingertip geometry: the pads sit roughly 0-4.5 cm below the reported eef_pos, so grasping a block on the z=0.80 table wants eef z about 0.82-0.86, and pushing the z command to the 0.80 clamp makes the fingers jam on the table and skids the hand sideways in y (I saw a 1.4 cm -y drift that cost the grasp). (5) Cameras: in the wrist view image-up is world +x and image-right is -y, and the block must be judged against the finger gap rather than the frame centre because the optical axis is offset forward; the two fixed cameras show almost no parallax for hand motion in x, so absolute x should be taken from the measured eef_pos plus the wrist view, not from them. (6) Layout: the block started near x=-0.045, y=0 and the bowl is centred near y=0 with its near wall around x=0.12; releasing at x=0.104 left the block on the table touching the outside of that wall, so the drop point needs to be nearer x=0.15-0.17 to clear the rim. (7) Budget: six calls spent localising the block was too many; the fast route is open wide, drive straight down onto the block with gripper=0 latched, confirm the opening stalls near 0.5, lift, translate over the bowl centre, then open.

hindsight: Rig facts I had to learn the hard way. hindsight: Concrete facts for a future agent on this rig. (1) Motion chunks: move_to returns a step count that is essentially set by the commanded distance divided by ~28 mm, and the arm only tracks ~4-10 mm per control step, so a plain position target typically yields 1-4 steps and moves the hand only 10-40 mm, far short of the target. Commanding an intermediate gripper value (0.4-0.5, which the adapter latches as hold-previous) is a reliable way to buy a long chunk without changing the grasp state. Plan every transport around this. (2) The reported gripper measurement is a good empty/closed discriminator: ~0.016 = closed on nothing, ~0.99 = fully open, an intermediate value would mean holding the block. (3) Geometry: table top z=0.80, the block is a ~30 mm cube, the bowl rim ~0.85. The fingertips sit roughly 50 mm BELOW the reported eef_pos, so eef z about 0.85 already puts the pads alongside a 30 mm block; do not waste calls descending further. (4) Vision: at 224x224 the fixed front and side views are nearly useless for metric servoing here - the hand moved 50-70 mm in the world for only a few pixels of image motion, so I could not settle whether each view horizontal is world x, world y or a diagonal, and my block estimates swung between (x +0.06, y -0.02) and (x -0.04, y -0.15). Best usable cue is the wrist camera, whose image right is roughly +x and image up roughly +y at ~1 mm/px near the centre, but its frame does NOT cover the volume directly under the fingertips: the block drops out of the bottom edge once the hand is within about 5 cm of it, which is easy to misread as alignment. (5) The bowl interior contains a small stationary red marker dot - do not mistake it for the red block being placed. (6) Repeated low slides with an open gripper visibly nudged the block (its front-view pixel drifted ~18 px over the trial), so approach from above and never sweep horizontally at table level. (7) Budget: 20 decisions is tight given the chunk behaviour; spend at most 3-4 on localisation, then grasp, lift, transport and release with gripper-change-driven long chunks.

hindsight: RIG FACTS worth more than the failed attempt. (1) STEP ACCOUNTING IS THE REAL CONSTRAINT: the number of control steps a move_to executes is set by the largest normalised dimension change - positions ~0.04 m/step, gripper ~0.0125/step, yaw ~0.3 rad/step. A pure 8 cm position command therefore buys only 2-3 steps and moves the arm a few mm, while toggling the gripper 0<->1 buys ~80 steps. Plan every long translation around a gripper toggle, and remember the toggle must land on the state you want. (2) The Cartesian servo lags at ~1-1.6 mm per control step, so budget ~100 steps per 10 cm of travel and count the total against 900 before choosing approach heights; my descent profile (1.00 -> 0.93 -> 0.906 -> 0.881 -> 1.005 -> 0.894) burned ~600 steps on vertical re-approaches. (3) Fingertips sit ~6.5 cm below eef_pos: at eef z=0.90 the pads are level with the top of a ~3.5 cm block and close on air; grasp a block on the 0.80 m table at eef z~0.87-0.88. (5) THE BOWL CONTAINS A SMALL RED DOT AT ITS CENTRE (a goal marker). From the wrist camera at low altitude it is the only red thing in frame and is trivially mistaken for the target block - check apparent size and context before steering at it. (6) The fixed front and side cameras are useless for localising along world x: a 13.7 cm x translation of the hand changed its image column by under 10 px in both views, so treat them as y/height references only. The wrist camera is the only usable x sensor, via parallax: fit the block image row against measured eef x (about 450 px/m at 15-20 cm standoff) rather than trying to read absolute positions. (7) The wrist camera axes are rotated relative to the arm: at yaw~0.05 image-up is roughly +x; rotating yaw by exactly pi/2 maps image-up to image-right, which is a cheap, grasp-neutral way (square block, jaws symmetric about the TCP) to disambiguate the axes - do that early, not at call 11. (9) Best sequence for this task given the budget: one call to hover above the block from a high vantage, one call to open+descend to z=0.875, one call to close, then lift only 3-4 cm (enough to clear the table) and go straight at the bowl in a single interpolated line, releasing by commanding gripper 1 while hovering above the rim.
